faq.a: They mean the same thing. 못 잊어 is shorter and more conversational, while 잊지 못해 sounds a bit more serious, as in song lyrics.

faq.q: How do you pronounce 못 잊어?
faq.a: Roughly mon-ni-jeo. The ㅅ of 못 becomes an n sound, and an extra ㄴ is added before 잊어.

intro: 기다릴게 (gidarilge) means "I'll wait" or "I'll wait for you." It is a promise you hear in romantic dramas and songs, and also in everyday plans like "I'll wait outside."
literal: It is 기다리다 (to wait) plus -ㄹ게, an ending for promising or telling someone what you will do for them. It is pronounced like 기다릴께, but the correct spelling is 기다릴게.
usage: Use it to promise something to the listener. It is casual, so say it to a partner or friend. The polite form is 기다릴게요.
In love stories it often means waiting for someone who is leaving, for example a partner going to military service or abroad.
Do not confuse it with 기다려, which means "Wait!" as a request or order.
To ask someone to wait for you, say 기다려 줘 ("Wait for me").

examples.context: Saying goodbye at the airport
Meeting a coworker after work
A girlfriend seeing her boyfriend off to the army
examples.en: Take care in the army. I'll wait for you.

faq.q: Is it 기다릴게 or 기다릴께?
faq.a: 기다릴게 is correct. It sounds like 께 when spoken, so 기다릴께 is a very common misspelling.

faq.q: What's the difference between 기다릴게 and 기다려?
faq.a: 기다릴게 is a promise: "I'll wait." 기다려 is a request or command: "Wait!"

intro: 결혼 (gyeolhon) means "marriage." You hear it in proposals like 나랑 결혼해 줄래? ("Will you marry me?") and in endless family pressure scenes in K-dramas.
literal: A Sino-Korean word: 결 (結, to tie) plus 혼 (婚, marriage). Literally "tying a marriage."
usage: The verb is 결혼하다 (to marry). The person you marry takes 와/과 or 랑, not an object marker: 너랑 결혼하고 싶어 ("I want to marry you").
Common proposals are 결혼하자 ("Let's get married") and 나랑 결혼해 줄래? ("Will you marry me?").
The wedding itself is 결혼식. Asking 결혼했어요? ("Are you married?") is a fairly common personal question in Korea.
Older expressions are 장가가다 (for a man) and 시집가다 (for a woman).

examples.context: A proposal
Sharing news with a coworker
Handing out wedding invitations
examples.en: Please be sure to come to the wedding.

faq.q: How do you say "Will you marry me?" in Korean?
faq.a: 나랑 결혼해 줄래? is the common casual way. 저랑 결혼해 주실래요? is a more polite version.

faq.q: What particle do you use with 결혼하다?
faq.a: Use 와/과 or 랑 for the person: 그 사람과 결혼했어요 ("I married that person"). Using 를 is a common learner mistake.

intro: 꽃미남 (kkotminam) means a "flower boy": a man with soft, pretty, almost delicate good looks. You hear it about actors and idols, in dramas and in fan talk.
literal: 꽃 means "flower" and 미남 means "handsome man." Put together, it is a man who is handsome in the way a flower is beautiful.
usage: It describes a specific kind of handsome: clear skin, fine features, a gentle or pretty face. A rugged, muscular man is more likely called 몸짱 or just 멋있다.
It is a compliment and can be used about anyone, from celebrities to a classmate. Saying it straight to a man's face is friendly and a little teasing.
Near-synonyms are 미남 (handsome man) and the slang 존잘 (super handsome). 꽃미남 adds the idea of pretty rather than tough.

forms.note: The plain word, without the flower image.
A common phrase in entertainment news.

examples.context: Gushing about an actor
examples.en: That actor is a real flower boy.

examples.context: Gossip at school
examples.en: I heard a flower-boy transfer student came to our school.

examples.context: Talking about your type
examples.en: I like a dependable guy more than a flower boy.

faq.q: Is kkotminam a compliment?
faq.a: Yes. It praises a man's good looks. It can sound a little teasing, but it is not an insult.

faq.q: What's the difference between kkotminam and momjjang?
faq.a: 꽃미남 is about a pretty face. 몸짱 is about a fit, muscular body. One person can be both.

intro: 막장 (makjang) describes something so outrageous it has hit rock bottom. 막장 드라마 is the name for melodramas full of affairs, birth secrets, slaps and revenge.
literal: In its original sense, 막장 is the far dead end of a mine tunnel, the deepest point where the digging happens. The slang meaning comes from that idea of reaching the very bottom.
usage: Most often it is about TV: 막장 드라마 means a drama with absurd, extreme plot twists that people complain about but keep watching.
It is also said about real behavior or situations that are shockingly bad, as in 막장이다 ("that's outrageous").
It is casual and critical. Calling someone's life or family 막장 to their face is insulting.

forms.note: Used when a story takes a wild turn.
Said about a plot or real behavior.

examples.context: Watching the evening drama
Admitting a guilty pleasure
examples.en: The plot is so makjang that I keep watching.

examples.context: Talking about your family
examples.en: My mom likes makjang dramas the most.

faq.q: What is a makjang drama?
faq.a: A drama with extreme, unrealistic plots: secret children, affairs, memory loss, revenge, family feuds. Many are daily or weekend dramas with high ratings.

faq.q: Is makjang always negative?
faq.a: Mostly it is a criticism. But fans also use it with affection for a show they enjoy because it is so wild.

intro: 출생의 비밀 (chulsaengui bimil) means "the secret of one's birth." It is the famous K-drama twist where a character's real parents turn out to be someone else.
literal: 출생 means "birth," 의 is the possessive particle ("of"), and 비밀 means "secret."
usage: It names a plot device more than an everyday phrase: babies switched at birth, a hidden child of a rich family, a lover who turns out to be a half sibling.
Viewers use it with a sigh or a laugh, as in 또 출생의 비밀이야? ("A birth secret again?"). It is closely linked to 막장 dramas.
In real life the phrase can be used seriously about adoption or family secrets, so take care when joking about it with someone you do not know well.

forms.note: A typical way a plot summary puts it.
Often the scene that reveals the secret.

examples.context: Rolling your eyes at a plot twist
Complaining about dramas
examples.en: Dramas always seem to have a birth secret.

examples.context: Explaining the twist to a friend
examples.en: It turns out there was a secret about his birth.

faq.q: Why are birth secrets so common in K-dramas?
faq.a: They create instant conflict about family, money and love, which drive many Korean melodramas. The twist is so common it has become a joke.

faq.q: Can I use chulsaengui bimil in normal conversation?
faq.a: Yes, usually jokingly about a drama. Used seriously, it refers to a real hidden fact about someone's parents.

intro: 실장님 (siljangnim) is a polite title for the head of an office or team. In K-dramas it is often the rich hero's capable right-hand man, and in real life it is also what you call a senior stylist at a hair salon.
literal: 실 means "room" or "office," 장 means "head" or "chief," and 님 is the honorific suffix. So it is roughly "respected head of the office."
usage: It is both a job title and a form of address. Staff call their boss 실장님, often with the surname: 김 실장님.
A superior drops 님 and says 김 실장. Saying it without 님 to your own boss would be rude.
Outside offices, salons, agencies and many small businesses use 실장 for senior staff, so customers say 실장님 too.
In dramas, 비서실장 (chief secretary) is a classic role: the loyal aide who knows all of the family's secrets.

forms.note: Used by superiors or when talking about someone.
Surname plus title is the usual way to address someone.

examples.context: A secretary reporting to her boss
examples.en: Sir, the meeting is all set.

examples.context: A chaebol heir giving an order
examples.en: Manager Kim, get the car ready.

examples.context: Booking at a hair salon
examples.en: I'd like to get a cut from the head stylist.

faq.q: What does siljangnim mean in English?
faq.a: It has no exact match. Depending on the setting it is translated as manager, director, chief, or head stylist.

faq.q: Why do drama characters keep saying siljangnim?
faq.a: Many dramas are set in big companies or rich families, where the hero has a trusted aide with the title 실장. The other characters address him by that title.

intro: 본부장님 (bonbujangnim) is a polite title for the head of a company division, often translated "director." In K-dramas the young, cold, rich heir is very often a 본부장.
literal: 본부 means "headquarters" or "main division," 장 means "head," and 님 is the honorific suffix.
usage: In real companies it is a senior executive title. Employees always address the person as 본부장님, often with the surname.
In romantic comedies, a chaebol son is commonly given this post so he can be both powerful and young. Viewers even joke about the 본부장 type of male lead.
Superiors such as the chairman may say 본부장 without 님, or call the person by name.

examples.context: An employee at the director's office
examples.en: Director, I brought the documents for your approval.

examples.context: Office gossip
examples.en: They say the new director is the chairman's son.

examples.context: Answering a phone call for the boss
examples.en: The director is out of the office today.

faq.q: What rank is a bonbujang?
faq.a: It is a senior management title above team leaders, heading a whole division. The exact rank depends on the company.

faq.q: Why is the male lead always a bonbujang?
faq.a: It lets a young heir hold real power before he takes over from his father, the 회장. It became a familiar romance setup.

intro: 회장님 (hoejangnim) means "Chairman" with respect. In K-dramas it is the powerful head of a conglomerate, usually the hero's father or grandfather.
literal: 회 means "association" or "group," 장 means "head," and 님 is the honorific suffix. So it is the respected head of an organization.
usage: It is the top title in a big company group, above 사장 and 대표. Everyone below addresses the person as 회장님.
회장 is also used for the head of any club or association, such as a student council president (학생회장). Members may jokingly call them 회장님.
Family members in dramas sometimes call the patriarch 회장님 too, which shows how cold or formal the family is.

forms.note: The same word in a school setting.

examples.context: A secretary summoning someone
examples.en: The chairman is asking for you.

examples.context: Visiting the elderly chairman
examples.en: Chairman, is your health a little better?

examples.context: Office gossip
examples.en: I hear the chairman's grandson is joining our company.

faq.q: What's the difference between hoejangnim and sajangnim?
faq.a: 회장님 is the chairman of a whole group. 사장님 is a company president, and also the everyday word for any shop or restaurant owner.

faq.q: Is hoejang only used for businesses?
faq.a: No. The head of a club, alumni group or student council is also a 회장.

intro: 대표님 (daepyonim) is a polite way to address the head of a company, often translated "CEO." In K-pop and dramas it is also what idols call the head of their agency.
literal: 대표 means "representative," and 님 is the honorific suffix. The title comes from 대표이사, the legal head of a company.
usage: Employees, clients and partners all address a company head as 대표님.
It feels more modern and corporate than 사장님. Startups, agencies and design studios usually use 대표, while 사장님 is also used for any shop owner.
대표 also means "representative" in general, as in 국가대표 (national team player), so context matters.

examples.context: Reminding the boss of a meeting
examples.en: CEO, it's almost time for the investor meeting.

examples.context: An idol sharing good news
examples.en: The head of our agency approved our debut.

examples.context: Praising your boss to a friend
examples.en: Our CEO is really good to the employees.

faq.q: What's the difference between daepyonim and sajangnim?
faq.a: Both can mean the boss of a company. 대표님 sounds more corporate and is common at startups and agencies. 사장님 is also used for restaurant and shop owners.

faq.q: Do K-pop idols call their agency head daepyonim?
faq.a: Yes. The head of an entertainment agency is usually called 대표님 by the artists and staff.

intro: 비서 (biseo) means "secretary" or "personal assistant." Boss and secretary romances are a familiar K-drama setup, so you hear lines like 김 비서 (Secretary Kim) a lot.
literal: 비서 is a Sino-Korean word made of 비 ("secret") and 서 ("writing, documents"), describing someone who handles confidential papers.
usage: Bosses usually call a secretary by surname plus title, like 김 비서, not by first name.
Other people talking to someone else's secretary may add 님 to be polite: 비서님.
In politics, 비서 and 비서관 are aides to lawmakers or the president, so the word is not only for office assistants.

forms.note: Surname plus title, how bosses address them.

examples.context: A boss starting the day
examples.en: Secretary Kim, what's on my schedule today?

examples.context: Introducing yourself on the phone
Before a meeting
examples.en: The secretary prepared the meeting materials.

faq.q: How do you address a secretary in Korean?
faq.a: Usually surname plus 비서, like 김 비서. If they are not your own secretary, 비서님 is more polite.

faq.q: Does biseo have another meaning?
faq.a: The same sound can be other Sino-Korean words, but in everyday speech 비서 almost always means a secretary.

intro: 도련님 (doryeonnim) means "young master." In dramas it is what servants call the unmarried son of a noble or rich family, and in real families a wife uses it for her husband's unmarried younger brother.
literal: 도련님 is the honorific form of 도령, an old word for an unmarried young man of good family. 님 adds respect.
usage: In historical dramas, servants call the young son of a yangban household 도련님. Chaebol dramas copy this with housekeepers calling the heir 도련님.
In modern family terms, a married woman calls her husband's younger, unmarried brother 도련님. Once he marries, the traditional term becomes 서방님.
Some people find these in-law terms outdated or unequal, since a husband's terms for his wife's siblings are less formal. Many families now use other terms, but 도련님 is still widely heard.
The female counterpart in both senses is 아가씨.

forms.note: The base word, as in old tales.
Also an old word for one's husband.

examples.context: A housekeeper in a rich family's mansion
A servant in a historical drama
examples.en: Young master, where are you going?

examples.context: A wife teasing her husband's younger brother
examples.en: When are you going to get married?

faq.q: Who do you call doryeonnim in a family?
faq.a: A married woman calls her husband's younger brother 도련님 while he is single. After he marries, the traditional term is 서방님.

faq.q: Is doryeonnim still used today?
faq.a: Yes, though some families find it old-fashioned and choose softer terms. In dramas it is very common for rich young heirs.

intro: 마마 (mama) is a royal honorific in historical dramas, attached to titles like 중전마마 (the queen) and 대비마마 (the queen dowager). It is not the word for mom.
literal: It is a title of respect used for royalty in the Joseon court. It is unrelated to the English word "mama," even though it sounds the same.
usage: Court ladies, eunuchs, officials and family members attach it to royal titles: 상감마마 (the king), 중전마마 (the queen), 대비마마 (the queen dowager).
Royal children call their parents 아바마마 (father) and 어마마마 (mother), which you hear often in sageuk.
Officials in court usually address the king as 전하. 상감마마 is more of a palace and household term.
Modern Koreans do not call their mother 마마; that is 엄마 or 어머니. The word 마마 also has an old meaning of smallpox, which you may see in historical stories.

forms.note: The king's mother or a former queen.
How a prince or princess addresses the queen.
How a prince or princess addresses the king.

examples.context: A court lady announcing the king
examples.en: Your Majesty, His Majesty has arrived.

examples.context: A prince greeting his mother in the morning
examples.en: Mother, your son comes to pay his respects.

examples.context: A court lady delivering a message
examples.en: The queen dowager is asking for you.

faq.q: Does mama mean mom in Korean?
faq.a: No. Mom is 엄마. 마마 is a royal honorific heard in historical dramas.

faq.q: What's the difference between mama and jeonha?
faq.a: 전하 is the direct address for the Joseon king, used by officials. 마마 is attached to royal titles, as in 중전마마 or 대비마마, and is used more inside the palace.

intro: 전하 (jeonha) is how officials address the king in Joseon-era historical dramas. Subtitles usually render it "Your Majesty."
literal: 전하 is Sino-Korean for "below the palace hall." Instead of naming the ruler directly, the speaker refers to the place beneath him.
usage: In Joseon, the king was addressed as 전하, not 폐하. 폐하 was reserved for emperors, and Joseon kings used the lower title in their relationship with China.
The crown prince was 저하, one step lower again. When translating European royalty, 전하 is used for princes and princesses, like "Your Highness."
It is formal court language, so it comes with archaic endings like -옵니다 and -시옵소서. It is never used in modern daily life except as a joke.

forms.note: Formal title, used in court announcements.
The address for the crown prince.

examples.context: A minister pleading in court
examples.en: Your Majesty, please reconsider this carefully.

examples.context: Officials objecting to the king's order
examples.en: Your Majesty, this must not be!

examples.context: A eunuch announcing the king's arrival

faq.q: What's the difference between jeonha and pyeha?
faq.a: 폐하 is for an emperor and 전하 is for a king. Joseon kings were addressed as 전하. Emperors of China and of the Korean Empire after 1897 were 폐하.

faq.q: Why do sageuk subtitles translate jeonha as Your Majesty?
faq.a: Because it is how a reigning king is addressed, and "Your Majesty" is the natural English equivalent, even though the word is technically one level below 폐하.

intro: 폐하 (pyeha) means "Your Majesty" for an emperor or empress. You hear it in dramas about emperors, Chinese courts and fantasy kingdoms, and in news about European monarchs.
literal: 폐하 is Sino-Korean for "below the steps," meaning the steps leading up to the throne. Like 전하, it avoids addressing the ruler directly.
usage: It is the highest form of address, used for emperors and empresses. In Korean history it applies to the emperors of the Korean Empire, proclaimed in 1897.
Joseon kings were addressed as the lower 전하, so using 폐하 in a Joseon-set drama would be a historical mistake.
Modern Korean news uses it for reigning monarchs abroad, such as 여왕 폐하 for a queen regnant.
It goes with formal court speech and is only used jokingly in everyday life.

examples.context: Crowds cheering at a coronation
examples.en: Long live His Majesty the Emperor!

examples.context: A general accepting an order
examples.en: Your Majesty, I will carry out your command.

examples.context: An attendant at the palace doors

faq.q: Did Korean kings use pyeha?
faq.a: Joseon kings did not; they were 전하. The title 폐하 was used for the emperors of the Korean Empire from 1897.

faq.q: Is pyeha higher than jeonha?
faq.a: Yes. 폐하 is for emperors and 전하 is for kings, one level lower.

intro: 사극 (sageuk) means a historical drama, usually set in the Joseon era or earlier. It is the genre with kings, court ladies, hanbok and lines like 전하.
literal: 사 means "history" and 극 means "drama" or "play."
usage: It covers TV dramas and films set in Korea's past. Many are set in Joseon, but Goryeo, the Three Kingdoms and other periods appear too.
Koreans often split the genre into 정통 사극, which tries to stay close to history, and 퓨전 사극, which mixes in romance, modern humor or fantasy.
사극 말투 means the old-fashioned court speech with endings like -하옵니다 and -하오. People imitate it for fun.

forms.note: Mixes history with modern or fantasy elements.

examples.context: Telling a friend about your new hobby
examples.en: I'm hooked on historical dramas these days.

examples.context: Praising an actor in hanbok
examples.en: This actor really suits historical dramas.

examples.context: A friend keeps talking like a court official

faq.q: What does sageuk mean?
faq.a: It means a historical drama. Most are set in the Joseon dynasty, but any Korean period drama counts.

faq.q: Are sageuk historically accurate?
faq.a: It varies. 정통 사극 tries to follow the records, while 퓨전 사극 freely adds fiction, romance and fantasy.

intro: 복수 (boksu) means "revenge." Revenge plots drive many K-dramas, and characters vow 복수할 거야 ("I'll get revenge") all the time.
literal: 복수 is a Sino-Korean word for paying back a wrong. A completely different word with the same spelling and sound, 복수, means "plural" in grammar.
usage: The verb is 복수하다, "to take revenge." You take revenge on someone with 에게 or 한테: 그 사람한테 복수할 거야.
A revenge drama is a 복수극. Viewers enjoy them for the 사이다 moment when the villain finally gets what they deserve.
In daily life it is often used lightly, for example about getting back at a friend in a game.

examples.context: A wronged heroine making a vow
examples.en: I will get revenge, no matter what.

examples.context: Recommending a show
examples.en: This drama is a revenge story, so it's really satisfying.

examples.context: An older character giving advice
examples.en: Revenge only leads to more revenge.

faq.q: How do you say "I will get revenge" in Korean?
faq.a: 복수할 거야 is casual. A stronger vow is 반드시 복수하겠어.

faq.q: Does boksu also mean plural?
faq.a: Yes, but that is a different word that happens to sound the same. In dramas and daily talk, 복수 usually means revenge.

intro: 운명 (unmyeong) means "fate" or "destiny." You hear it all the time in K-drama romances, when two people keep running into each other and one of them finally says 운명이야, "it's fate."
literal: 운명 is a Sino-Korean word written 運命. 운 (運) means luck or fortune, and 명 (命) means life or one's lot in life.
usage: It is a normal, everyday word, not only a drama word. People use it for love, for big life events and for things that feel meant to happen.
In romance stories it is often said almost as a confession: 우리는 운명이야 means "we are meant to be." Said seriously in real life, it can sound dramatic or cheesy.
운명적 means "fateful" and is used before nouns, as in 운명적인 만남 (a fateful meeting).
Compare 인연, which is the connection or bond between people. 운명 is the larger force that decides what happens.

forms.note: 운명적 + 인 turns it into a describing word.

forms.en: the one you are destined for

forms.note: Heavier word, for a fate you cannot escape.

examples.context: Two leads meet again by chance
Asking someone on a date what they think
Telling a friend how you met your partner again

faq.q: How do you say "it's fate" in Korean?
faq.a: Say 운명이야 (unmyeong-iya) casually, or 운명이에요 (unmyeong-ieyo) politely. 운명인가 봐 means "I guess it's fate."

faq.q: What is the difference between unmyeong and inyeon?
faq.a: 운명 is fate or destiny in general. 인연 is the bond or connection between two people. You might say two people with a strong 인연 were brought together by 운명.

intro: 인연 (inyeon) means a connection or bond between people, often one that feels meant to be. In K-dramas you hear lines like 우리 인연인가 봐, "I guess we're connected," and sad ones like 인연이 아닌가 봐, "I guess we're not meant to be."
literal: 인연 is a Sino-Korean word written 因緣. 因 means cause and 緣 means tie or connection. It is a Buddhist idea: meetings between people have causes that reach beyond chance.
usage: It covers all kinds of relationships, not only romance. Friends, teachers, coworkers and even a stranger you share a nice moment with can be a 인연.
좋은 인연 is a good connection, and people often thank someone for it when a project or job ends.
인연이 아니다 ("not meant to be") is a gentle way to talk about a relationship that did not work out.
A famous saying is 옷깃만 스쳐도 인연, "even brushing sleeves is a connection," meaning no meeting is meaningless.

forms.note: The opposite of a good 인연.
Used for couples who are perfect for each other.
Said after a breakup or a missed chance.

examples.context: Bumping into the same person for the third time
examples.en: I guess we're meant to meet.

examples.context: After a breakup, talking to yourself
examples.en: I guess we just weren't meant to be.

examples.context: A stranger you just met offers to eat together
examples.en: Since fate brought us together, let's have a meal.

faq.q: Is inyeon only about romance?
faq.a: No. 인연 can be any meaningful connection: friends, family, teachers, coworkers. It is common in romance dramas, but Koreans use it widely.

faq.q: What does inyeon-i anin-ga bwa mean?
faq.a: 인연이 아닌가 봐 means "I guess we're not meant to be." People say it when a relationship ends or keeps failing to happen.

intro: 귀신 (gwisin) means "ghost." It is the everyday Korean word for a spirit of the dead, and you hear it in horror films, ghost dramas and scary stories told at night.
literal: 귀신 is a Sino-Korean word written 鬼神. 鬼 means ghost and 神 means spirit or god.
usage: It is the normal word for a ghost and can be used by anyone. Kids, adults and news reports all say 귀신.
The best known type in Korean horror is the 처녀귀신, the ghost of a young unmarried woman, usually shown with long black hair and a white dress.
귀신같이 ("like a ghost") means uncannily or perfectly, as in 귀신같이 알아, "knows it uncannily well."
Do not mix it up with 도깨비, a goblin-like folk creature. A 귀신 is the spirit of someone who died.

forms.note: The classic long-haired ghost of Korean horror.

examples.context: Walking into an old, empty school at night
examples.en: It feels like a ghost could show up here.

examples.context: A friend comes back pale from the bathroom
Your mother always finds out what you did

faq.q: What is a cheonyeo gwisin?
faq.a: 처녀귀신 is the ghost of a young woman who died unmarried. In Korean horror she usually has long black hair and a white mourning dress, and is often said to haunt because of her unresolved grief.

faq.q: Is a gwisin the same as a dokkaebi?
faq.a: No. A 귀신 is the spirit of a dead person. A 도깨비 is a folk creature, more like a goblin, known for tricks and magic rather than haunting.

intro: 도깨비 (dokkaebi) is a creature from Korean folklore, usually translated as "goblin." Many English speakers know the word from the 2016 drama Guardian: The Lonely and Great God, whose Korean title is simply 도깨비.
literal: 도깨비 is a native Korean word, not Sino-Korean. Its exact origin is not certain.
usage: In folk tales a 도깨비 is not a ghost of the dead. It is a mischievous being that plays tricks, loves to wrestle, and can reward good people or punish greedy ones.
Its best known item is the 도깨비방망이, a magic club that makes things appear when struck. People mention it when wishing for something impossible.
The word also appears in compounds: 도깨비불 is a strange floating light like a will-o'-the-wisp.
It is the same word in casual and polite speech. Only the ending of the sentence changes.

forms.note: Strikes the ground to make wishes come true.
A mysterious light seen at night.
A different being: the spirit of a dead person.

examples.context: A character in a fantasy drama sees something strange
Wishing for an easy way out of your problems
examples.en: I wish I had a dokkaebi's magic club.

examples.context: Talking about childhood bedtime stories
examples.en: I often heard dokkaebi stories when I was little.

faq.q: Is a dokkaebi a ghost?
faq.a: No. A 귀신 is the spirit of someone who died, while a 도깨비 is a separate folk being. In many tales dokkaebi are playful or even helpful, not scary.

faq.q: Why is the drama Guardian also called Goblin?
faq.a: Its Korean title is 도깨비, and "goblin" is the usual English translation of that word, so many fans call it Goblin.

intro: 구미호 (gumiho) is the nine-tailed fox of Korean folklore, a fox that can turn into a beautiful woman. It is a favorite figure in fantasy K-dramas, where a gumiho often longs to become human.
literal: 구미호 is a Sino-Korean word written 九尾狐: 구 (九) means nine, 미 (尾) means tail and 호 (狐) means fox.
usage: In traditional tales the gumiho is a fox that has lived a very long time, often said to be a thousand years, and takes the form of a woman to trick people. Many stories say it eats human livers or hearts.
A common story line is that a gumiho can become fully human if it meets certain conditions, which is why modern dramas often make it a tragic or romantic character.
Calling a real person 구미호 means they are sly and seductive. It is not a compliment. The shorter 여우 (fox) is used the same way.

forms.note: Common word for a cunning charmer.
What makes a gumiho a gumiho.

examples.context: Explaining Korean folklore to a friend
Summing up the plot of a fantasy drama
examples.en: The gumiho wants to become human.

examples.context: Gossiping about a charming, scheming character
examples.en: That woman is a total fox.

faq.q: Does a gumiho really eat livers?
faq.a: In many traditional tales, yes: the gumiho eats human livers or hearts, sometimes to become human. Modern dramas often soften this or turn it into a dark backstory.

faq.q: Is it rude to call someone a gumiho?
faq.a: It can be. Calling someone 구미호 or 여우 suggests they are sly and use charm to manipulate people. Among friends it can be teasing, but it is not praise.

intro: 저승사자 (jeoseungsaja) means "grim reaper," the messenger who comes to lead the dead to the afterlife. In K-dramas and films he usually appears in a black hat and a long black robe.
literal: 저승 is the world of the dead, the opposite of 이승, the world of the living. 사자 (使者) means messenger. Together: "messenger of the afterlife."
usage: In Korean belief the 저승사자 comes to take a person's soul when their time is up and guides it to the afterlife.
People joke that someone dressed all in black or looking very pale looks like a 저승사자.
저승 on its own shows up in casual talk too: 저승 갈 뻔했어 means "I almost died," usually said as an exaggeration.
Note that 사자 here means messenger. The same sound 사자 also means lion, but that is a different word.

forms.en: the afterlife, world of the dead
this world, the world of the living

examples.context: A scene from a fantasy drama
examples.en: The grim reaper has come to take him.

examples.context: Your friend shows up wearing all black
examples.en: In those black clothes you look like a grim reaper.

examples.context: Telling a friend about a bad night
examples.en: I had a dream about a grim reaper.

faq.q: What does a jeoseungsaja look like?
faq.a: In modern dramas and films he usually wears a black gat (a traditional wide-brimmed hat) and a black robe, with a pale face. Older folk beliefs describe reapers in several different ways.

faq.q: What is jeoseung?
faq.a: 저승 is the afterlife, the world where the dead go. Its opposite is 이승, this world of the living.

intro: 계약 결혼 (gyeyak gyeolhon) means "contract marriage," a marriage two people agree to for practical reasons, usually with rules and an end date. It is one of the best known K-drama tropes, and the couple almost always falls in love for real.
literal: 계약 (契約) means contract and 결혼 (結婚) means marriage. It is often written as one word, 계약결혼.
usage: In dramas the reason is usually money, family pressure to marry, inheritance or a visa, and the deal comes with a written list of rules.
It is mostly a story device. A real legal marriage in Korea is a registration, and a secret private deal about it is not a recognized kind of marriage.
Do not confuse it with 정략결혼, a marriage arranged between two families for business or power, which is also common in chaebol dramas.
위장 결혼 means a sham marriage, usually one done to cheat the law, and has a more negative, criminal feel.

forms.note: Same thing, written as one word.
Usually illegal, for example for a visa.

examples.context: A rich heir makes an offer to the heroine
examples.en: Would you do a contract marriage with me?

examples.context: The heroine reminds herself not to fall in love
examples.en: This is just a contract marriage.

examples.context: Setting the terms of the deal

faq.q: Is contract marriage real in Korea?
faq.a: Mostly it is a fiction trope. A real marriage is a legal registration, and the secret contracts in dramas are a plot device rather than something the law recognizes.

faq.q: What is the difference between gyeyak gyeolhon and jeongnyak gyeolhon?
faq.a: 계약 결혼 is a deal between the two people marrying. 정략결혼 is a marriage arranged by families for business or power, where the couple may have little say.

intro: 꽃길 (kkotgil) means "flower path" and stands for a happy, easy future. Fans often tell idols 꽃길만 걷자, "let's walk only on flower paths," and you also hear it in dramas and congratulation messages.
literal: 꽃 means flower and 길 means road or path. Together: a road covered in flowers.
usage: It is used to wish someone a smooth, happy life or career, especially at a new start such as a debut, a graduation or a wedding.
꽃길만 걷자 ("let's walk only on flower paths") is a famous fan phrase. Fans also promise idols 꽃길만 걷게 해 줄게, "we'll make sure you only walk on flower paths."
People joke about the opposite, 흙길 (dirt road), for a hard, rough path.
It is warm and positive, and it suits both casual and polite speech.

forms.en: let's walk only on flower paths
forms.note: Famous wish between fans and idols.

forms.en: may you walk only on flower paths

examples.context: Fans cheering for an idol group's new start
examples.en: From now on, let's walk only on flower paths!

examples.context: A fan's banner at a concert
examples.en: We'll make sure you only walk on flower paths.

examples.context: Texting a friend on graduation day
examples.en: Congrats on graduating. I hope only good things come your way.

faq.q: What does kkotgilman geotja mean?
faq.a: 꽃길만 걷자 means "let's walk only on flower paths," a wish for a happy future together. It is very common between K-pop fans and their idols.

faq.q: Is kkotgil only used for idols?
faq.a: No. Anyone can wish someone a 꽃길: a friend starting a job, a couple getting married or a student graduating.

intro: 사이다 (saida) literally means a clear lemon-lime soda, but in slang it means a satisfying, refreshing moment, like when a drama character finally tells off the villain. Viewers comment 완전 사이다, "so satisfying," when that happens.
literal: 사이다 comes from the English word "cider," but in Korea it means a clear, fizzy lemon-lime soda like Sprite. The slang sense comes from the cool, fizzy relief of drinking one after something heavy.
usage: The slang meaning is used for scenes, comments and actions that release built-up frustration: a sharp comeback, a long-awaited revenge, a bad boss getting caught.
Common combinations are 사이다 발언 (a satisfying remark) and 사이다 전개 (a satisfying plot turn).
Its opposite is 고구마 (sweet potato), for frustrating moments that feel stuck in your throat.
The soda meaning is still normal, so 사이다 주세요 at a restaurant just gets you a drink.

forms.note: Someone says what everyone wanted to say.

examples.context: Talking about last night's episode
The heroine finally talks back to her mother-in-law
A drama that dragged on finally picks up
examples.en: It was so frustrating, but finally a satisfying turn.

faq.q: Does saida just mean soda?
faq.a: Both. Literally it is a clear lemon-lime soda. In slang it means something satisfying that clears built-up frustration, and context tells you which one is meant.

faq.q: What is the opposite of saida?
faq.a: 고구마 (sweet potato). A 고구마 situation is frustrating and stuffy, and a 사이다 moment is the relief that clears it.

intro: 고구마 (goguma) literally means "sweet potato," but in slang it describes a frustrating situation or character that makes you want to scream. K-drama viewers use it when a plot drags or a lead keeps making painful choices.
literal: The slang comes from the feeling of eating dry sweet potato without water: it gets stuck in your throat and feels stuffy. 고구마 itself is the ordinary word for sweet potato.
usage: It is used for plots that drag, characters who never speak up, and misunderstandings that go on too long.
A 고구마 캐릭터 is a frustrating character, and 고구마 전개 is a frustrating stretch of plot.
People exaggerate with 고구마 백 개 먹은 것 같아, "I feel like I ate a hundred sweet potatoes."
Its opposite is 사이다 (soda), the refreshing moment that clears the frustration.

forms.note: Someone who keeps making things worse.

examples.context: Watching the lead stay silent again
examples.en: Why is the main character like that? So frustrating.

examples.context: Complaining after a long misunderstanding plot
examples.en: I feel like I ate a hundred sweet potatoes.

examples.context: Reviewing a drama with a friend
examples.en: The frustrating part of this drama drags on way too long.

faq.q: Why does sweet potato mean frustrating?
faq.a: Eating dry sweet potato without a drink makes your throat feel blocked and stuffy. That feeling is compared to being stuck with a frustrating situation.

faq.q: Is it rude to call someone goguma?
faq.a: It is teasing more than insulting. Calling a friend 고구마 means they are frustrating to watch, for example because they never say what they want.

intro: 짠하다 (jjanhada) describes the small ache you feel when you see someone in a sad or pitiful situation, like "it tugs at my heart" or "I feel for them." You hear it when characters watch a parent struggling or a friend eating alone.
literal: 짠하다 is a native Korean adjective made of 짠 plus 하다. Do not confuse it with 짜다 (to be salty) or the sound 짠! used for "ta-da" and "cheers."
usage: It mixes pity, sympathy and affection. It is often about people you care about, such as aging parents or a hardworking friend.
It is commonly used with 마음: 마음이 짠하다, "my heart aches."
It is softer than 불쌍하다 (pitiful), which can sound like you are looking down on someone.
In casual speech it is often shortened to 짠해 or 짠하네.

examples.context: Talking about a sad drama scene
examples.en: Watching that scene made my heart ache.

examples.context: Seeing a coworker eat alone at their desk
examples.en: Seeing him eat alone makes me feel a bit sorry for him.

examples.context: Watching your father walk home tired
examples.en: Why does Dad look so sad from behind?

faq.q: Is jjanhada the same as jjan (cheers)?
faq.a: No. 짠! is the sound for "cheers" or "ta-da." 짠하다 is an adjective for feeling a pang of sympathy.

faq.q: What is the difference between jjanhada and bulssanghada?
faq.a: Both mean you feel sorry for someone. 불쌍하다 means pitiful and can sound like you look down on them. 짠하다 is warmer and often comes with affection.

intro: 오글거려 (ogeulgeoryeo) means "that's cringey" or "it makes me cringe." People say it about cheesy love lines, over-the-top aegyo or embarrassing old social media posts.
literal: It comes from 오글거리다, whose sound suggests something curling or crinkling up. The cringe sense is linked to 손발이 오그라들다, "my hands and feet curl up," the physical feeling of second-hand embarrassment.
usage: It is casual. Friends say it to each other, often laughing, when someone says something cheesy.
The fuller expression 손발이 오글거려 ("my hands and feet are curling") makes it stronger.
It is not mean in itself, but telling someone their sincere confession is 오글거려 can hurt.
The polite form is 오글거려요.

forms.en: my hands and feet curl up
forms.note: Strong way to say something is cringey.

examples.context: Your friend reads out a cheesy love letter
Reacting to a drama confession scene
examples.en: Lines like that are so cringey.

examples.context: Looking at your old social media posts
examples.en: It's so cringey I can't even look.

faq.q: How do you say "cringe" in Korean?
faq.a: 오글거려 is the most common way. 손발이 오그라들어 is a stronger version, meaning "my hands and feet are curling up."

faq.q: Is ogeulgeoryeo rude?
faq.a: Not really. It is playful among friends. Just be careful saying it about someone's sincere feelings, since it can sound like mockery.

intro: 죽을래 (jugeullae) means "do you want to die?" It is a mock threat, usually said between siblings or close friends when someone is annoying them. You hear 너 죽을래? a lot in K-drama arguments.
literal: It is 죽다 (to die) plus the ending -을래, which asks what someone wants to do. Literally: "Will you die?" or "Do you want to die?"
usage: Among close friends and siblings it is usually a joking threat, similar to "you're dead" or "do you want me to kill you?" in English.
It is still rude and aggressive. Never say it to elders, bosses, strangers or anyone you are not very close to.
Said seriously or by a stranger, it sounds like a real threat.
A milder version is 맞을래? ("do you want to get hit?"), which is still only for close, casual relationships.

forms.en: Do you want to get hit?

forms.note: More direct and can sound harsher.

examples.context: Your little brother keeps poking you
You find your snacks gone
examples.en: You ate my snacks again, didn't you? You want to die?

examples.context: A friend teases you one time too many
examples.en: Hey, seriously, do you want to die?

faq.q: Is jugeullae a real threat?
faq.a: Usually not. Between siblings and close friends it is an exaggerated way to say "stop it." From a stranger, or said in anger, it can be a real threat.

faq.q: Can I say jugeullae to my Korean friends?
faq.a: Only to very close friends your own age or younger who already talk to you this way. It is rude, so never use it with elders or people you just met.

intro: 꺼져 (kkeojyeo) means "get lost" or "go away," and it is very rude. In K-dramas it is shouted at an ex, a rival or an unwanted visitor.
literal: It comes from 꺼지다, which normally means for a light or fire to go out. As a command to a person, it means "disappear."
usage: It is a harsh insult, close to "get lost" or "piss off." Saying it to anyone you are not very close to will start a fight.
Close friends sometimes use it jokingly, but it is never acceptable with elders, coworkers or strangers.
There is no polite form for this meaning. To ask someone to leave politely, say 나가 주세요 (please leave).
In ordinary use 꺼지다 is neutral: 불이 꺼졌어 just means "the light went out."

forms.en: to go out (light, fire); get lost

examples.context: A character throws out an ex who shows up uninvited
Shouting at a rival in a fight scene
examples.en: Get out of my sight right now.

examples.context: During a storm at home

faq.q: How rude is kkeojyeo?
faq.a: Very rude. It is like "get lost" or "piss off" in English and is used in real anger. Avoid it unless you are joking with a very close friend.

faq.q: Does kkeojyeo also mean turn off?
faq.a: The verb 꺼지다 means a light or machine goes off by itself, as in 불이 꺼졌어. To turn something off yourself, Koreans say 끄다, as in 불 꺼 (turn off the light).

intro: 내가 왜 (naega wae) means "Why should I?" or "Why me?" You hear it in K-dramas when a character flatly refuses to do something, or asks why something happened to them.
literal: 내가 is 나 (I) plus the subject particle 가, and 왜 means "why." Put together, it is literally "I, why?"
usage: The most common use is refusing: someone tells you to apologize or help, and you answer 내가 왜? meaning "Why would I?" It often sounds stubborn or annoyed.
It also starts a regretful question about yourself, as in 내가 왜 그랬을까? (Why did I do that?).
It is casual speech. To someone older or above you, the polite version is 제가 왜요?, though it can still sound defiant.
Compare 왜 alone, which simply asks "why?" Adding 내가 puts the focus on yourself: why should it be me?

forms.note: Uses the humble 제가 and the polite 요.
Said with regret about your own action.
Asks why something happened to you.

examples.context: Told to apologize first after a fight
Lying in bed regretting a text you sent
Denying a friend's teasing

faq.q: Is 내가 왜 rude?
faq.a: It is casual and can sound defiant, so it may come across as rude to a parent, teacher or boss. Between friends it is normal.

faq.q: What is the difference between 내가 왜 and 왜?
faq.a: 왜 just asks "why?" 내가 왜 asks "why me?" or "why should I?", so it is usually a refusal or a complaint.

intro: 이게 뭐야 (ige mwoya) means "What is this?" In K-dramas it is also a cry of disbelief, like "What the heck is this?", when a character sees a mess or a shocking result.
literal: 이게 is a shortened form of 이것이 (this thing + subject particle). 뭐야 is 뭐 (what) plus 야, the casual form of "is." So it is literally "This is what?"
usage: It can be a real question, for example when you open a box and do not know what is inside.
Said with a sharp tone, it shows surprise, annoyance or disappointment, like seeing a messy room or a bad test score.
It is casual. The polite version is 이게 뭐예요?, and the very formal one is 이것은 무엇입니까?
Compare 뭐야 alone, which works as "What?" or "What the..." without pointing at a specific thing.

forms.note: For strangers, staff or people older than you.
이건 adds a contrast, for the next item.

examples.context: Opening a surprise gift from a friend
A parent walking into a very messy room
examples.en: What is this? Why is the room like this?

examples.context: Seeing an unfamiliar dish at a market
examples.en: What is this? It's a food I've never seen.

faq.q: How do you say "What is this?" politely in Korean?
faq.a: Say 이게 뭐예요? (ige mwoyeyo). It is the safe choice with strangers, shop staff and anyone older than you.

faq.q: Why does 이게 뭐야 sound angry in dramas?
faq.a: The words are neutral, but a sharp tone turns it into "What is this supposed to be?" The tone, not the words, carries the anger.

intro: 설마 (seolma) means "No way" or "Surely not." In K-dramas you hear it when a character starts to suspect something they do not want to be true, like "Don't tell me..."
literal: 설마 is a native Korean adverb. It is a single word with no smaller parts, and it expresses doubt that something, usually bad, could really be true.
usage: It often stands alone with a trailing pause, 설마..., when a character realizes something shocking.
At the start of a question it means "Don't tell me..." or "Surely you didn't...", as in 설마 잊어버린 거 아니지?
The word itself is neutral, so you can use it in polite sentences too: 설마 벌써 가세요? (Surely you're not leaving already?).
Compare 혹시, which means "by any chance" and is neutral or hopeful. 설마 suggests you fear or doubt the answer.

forms.note: On its own, as a reaction.

forms.en: I thought there was no way, but...
forms.note: Used when the unlikely thing turns out true.
A proverb: do not ignore a risk just because it seems unlikely.

examples.context: A detective looking at new evidence
examples.en: Don't tell me that person is the culprit?

examples.context: Noticing a friend's eyes are wet
Reminding your partner about your anniversary

faq.q: What is the difference between 설마 and 혹시?
faq.a: 혹시 means "by any chance" and is a neutral way to ask. 설마 means "surely not" and shows you doubt or fear the answer.

faq.q: What does 설마가 사람 잡는다 mean?
faq.a: It is a proverb, roughly "'surely not' catches people." It warns that thinking a bad thing will never happen is exactly how it happens to you.

intro: 갑분싸 (gapbunssa) means the mood suddenly turned awkward or cold. Young Koreans say it online and among friends when a joke falls flat or someone says the wrong thing.
literal: It is short for 갑자기 분위기 싸해짐, "the atmosphere suddenly went cold." 갑 comes from 갑자기 (suddenly), 분 from 분위기 (mood), and 싸 from 싸하다, a chilly, uneasy feeling.
usage: It describes the moment a fun conversation dies, for example after a bad joke or an awkward question.
People say 갑분싸 됐다 (it got awkward) or 갑분싸 만들지 마 (don't kill the mood).
It is casual slang for friends and social media. Do not use it with older people or at work in formal situations.
A plain, non-slang way to say something similar is 분위기 깨다 (to ruin the mood).

forms.note: The most common way to use it.
Said about the person who caused it.
The plain, unshortened way to say it.

examples.context: Everyone goes quiet at a party
examples.en: Why did it suddenly get so awkward?

examples.context: Admitting your joke flopped
examples.en: It got awkward because of my joke.

examples.context: Warning a friend before a group dinner

faq.q: What does 갑분싸 stand for?
faq.a: 갑자기 분위기 싸해짐, meaning "the mood suddenly went cold." Each syllable comes from one of those words.

faq.q: Can I use 갑분싸 with my Korean teacher?
faq.a: Better not in class or in formal talk. It is playful slang among friends and online.

meaning: So annoying / It ticks me off
intro: 킹받네 (kingbatne) means "That's so annoying" or "That really ticks me off." Young Koreans use it online and with friends, often jokingly, when something is irritating in a funny way.
literal: It is a play on 열받네 (I'm getting mad, from 열받다, literally "to receive heat"). 열 is swapped for 킹, the English word "king," which Korean slang uses to mean "extremely."
usage: It is usually playful. People say it about a smug face, a teasing friend or a game they keep losing, not about something truly upsetting.
You will see it as 킹받네, 킹받아 or 킹받게 하네 (it makes me so mad).
It is not a swear word, but it is casual slang. Do not use it with elders, a boss or in formal settings.
For real anger, people are more likely to say 열받아 or 짜증나.

forms.en: You're really getting on my nerves.
forms.note: Blames someone or something for it.
The original phrase it plays on.

examples.context: Losing the same game level again
Looking at a friend's smug selfie
A friend keeps teasing you
examples.en: Stop trying to make me mad.

faq.q: Is 킹받네 a bad word?
faq.a: No. It is slang, not a curse. It is still too casual for elders, teachers or work.

faq.q: What is the difference between 킹받네 and 짜증나?
faq.a: 짜증나 is a general "I'm annoyed." 킹받네 is newer slang and usually sounds playful, like being annoyed in a funny way.

intro: 존잘 (jonjal) means "super handsome" or "really hot." It is internet slang that K-pop and K-drama fans use about good-looking actors, idols and guys they see online.
literal: It is short for 존나 잘생김 or 존나 잘생겼다. 존나 is a vulgar intensifier, roughly like "f***ing" in English, and 잘생기다 means "to be good-looking."
usage: It is used mostly about men, and mostly online or among close friends. 존잘남 means "super handsome guy."
Because 존 comes from a vulgar word, it is crude slang. Many young people use it lightly, but never say it to elders, teachers or at work.
Safer ways to say the same thing are 진짜 잘생겼다 (really handsome) or 완전 잘생겼다.
The matching word for a pretty woman or thing is 존예.

forms.note: Adds -러, a slang suffix for a person.

examples.context: Fans looking at a new drama poster
Asking a friend about her blind date
Asking for a drama recommendation
examples.en: Recommend me a drama with a super handsome male lead.

faq.q: Is 존잘 a bad word?
faq.a: It comes from 존나, a vulgar intensifier, so it is crude. Young people use it casually online, but avoid it with anyone you need to be polite to.

faq.q: Can you say 존잘 about a woman?
faq.a: It is mostly used for men. For women, people usually say 존예.

intro: 존예 (jonye) means "super pretty" or "gorgeous." It is internet slang for good-looking women, outfits, photos and even places, common in fan comments and chats.
literal: It is short for 존나 예쁨 or 존나 예쁘다. 존나 is a vulgar intensifier, roughly like "f***ing" in English, and 예쁘다 means "to be pretty."
usage: It is used about women, but also about things: a cafe, a photo or a dress can be 존예.
Because 존 comes from a vulgar word, it is crude slang. Keep it for close friends and online, never elders, teachers or work.
Safer ways to say it are 진짜 예쁘다 or 완전 예쁘다.
The matching word for a handsome man is 존잘.

forms.note: Common way to end a comment.
The safe version for any setting.

examples.context: Complimenting a close friend
Walking into a new cafe
Checking photos after a trip
examples.en: I got a really pretty photo!

faq.q: Is 존예 rude?
faq.a: Not to the person you describe, since it is a compliment. But the 존 part comes from a vulgar word, so it is too crude for polite company.

faq.q: What is the difference between 존예 and 예뻐?
faq.a: 예뻐 simply means "pretty" and is fine almost anywhere. 존예 is crude slang meaning "extremely pretty."

intro: 핵인싸 (haeginssa) means a super popular, super social person, the life of the party. Young Koreans use it online and in daily talk for someone everyone seems to know.
literal: 핵 means "nuclear" and is a slang prefix for "extremely." 인싸 comes from the English word "insider" and means a popular, socially active person. So 핵인싸 is an "extreme insider."
usage: It is usually a compliment or a friendly tease: 걔 완전 핵인싸야 (She's a total social butterfly).
It can also describe trendy things that popular people like, such as 핵인싸 아이템 (a must-have item for cool kids).
The opposite is 아싸, an "outsider" who keeps to themselves.
It is casual slang, fine with friends and online but odd in formal speech.

examples.context: Describing a classmate who knows everyone
Explaining a new app trend
examples.en: All the popular kids use this app.

examples.context: Starting at a new school
examples.en: I want to be super popular too.

faq.q: What is the difference between 인싸 and 핵인싸?
faq.a: 핵인싸 is a stronger 인싸. 핵 works like "mega" or "super," so 핵인싸 is someone extremely popular and social.

faq.q: Is 핵인싸 a compliment?
faq.a: Usually, yes. It can be a light tease, but it is not an insult.

intro: 꿀팁 (kkultip) means a great tip or a useful life hack. You see it everywhere in Korean YouTube titles, blogs and chats, like 여행 꿀팁 (travel tips).
literal: 꿀 means "honey" and 팁 is the English word "tip." In slang, 꿀 means something sweet and very good, as in 꿀잼 (super fun) and 꿀잠 (sweet sleep).
usage: It is light slang but very widespread, so even companies and TV shows use it in titles.
People say 꿀팁 하나 알려 줄게 (Let me give you a great tip) or 이거 완전 꿀팁이다 (This is such a good tip).
Unlike crude slang, it is safe almost anywhere. In very formal writing, 유용한 팁 (useful tip) is more neutral.
Other 꿀 words include 꿀잼 (super fun) and 꿀템 (great item).

examples.context: About to show a friend a shortcut
examples.en: Let me tell you a great tip.

examples.context: Reading a clever cleaning trick online
examples.en: This is a really great tip!

examples.context: Planning a trip to Seoul

faq.q: Is 꿀팁 rude or vulgar?
faq.a: No. It is friendly, harmless slang that even TV shows and brands use.

faq.q: Why does 꿀 mean "good" in Korean slang?
faq.a: 꿀 means honey. Slang uses it for anything sweet or rewarding, like 꿀잼 (super fun) and 꿀잠 (a really good sleep).

intro: 멘붕 (menbung) means a mental breakdown in the everyday sense: freaking out, panicking or your mind going blank. Koreans use it in chats, variety shows and daily talk.
literal: It is short for 멘탈 붕괴, "mental collapse." 멘탈 is the English word "mental," and 붕괴 means "collapse."
usage: It is used for everyday shocks, like losing your phone, seeing a hard exam question or a sudden change of plans.
Common phrases are 멘붕이야 (I'm freaking out), 멘붕 왔어 (I lost it) and 멘붕에 빠지다 (to fall into panic).
It is casual but not rude, and many adults use it. In serious talk about mental health, use real terms instead.
Near-synonyms are 어떡해 (what do I do?) and 큰일 났어 (I'm in big trouble).

examples.context: Realizing a deadline is today
examples.en: I'm totally freaking out right now.

examples.context: After a tough exam
examples.en: I saw the questions and my mind went blank.

examples.context: Telling a coworker politely
examples.en: I lost my phone, so I'm panicking.

faq.q: What does 멘붕 stand for?
faq.a: 멘탈 붕괴, which means "mental collapse." In everyday talk it just means you are panicking or overwhelmed.

faq.q: Is 멘붕 a serious word?
faq.a: No. It is used for everyday shocks and is often funny. It is not a medical term.

intro: 극혐 (geukhyeom) means "so gross" or "I really can't stand it." It is strong internet slang that Koreans use about things they find disgusting, like bugs or a food they hate.
literal: It is a shortening of 극혐오, "extreme disgust." 극 means "extreme" and 혐 comes from 혐오, which means disgust or loathing.
usage: It is common about things: 바퀴벌레 극혐 (cockroaches are the worst).
It is a harsh word. Using it about a person or a group of people sounds hateful and offensive, so avoid that.
It is casual slang. Never use it in polite or formal settings.
Milder ways to say you dislike something are 싫어 (I don't like it) and 별로야 (not great).

forms.note: The standard word it comes from.

examples.context: Seeing a bug in the kitchen
Arguing about ice cream flavors
examples.en: Mint chocolate is disgusting to me.

examples.context: Complaining about rude comments online
examples.en: I really can't stand stuff like this.

faq.q: Is 극혐 offensive?
faq.a: It can be. About things like bugs it is just strong slang. About people, it sounds hateful and many Koreans find it offensive.

faq.q: What is a softer word than 극혐?
faq.a: 싫어 (I don't like it) or 별로야 (it's not great) say you dislike something without sounding harsh.

intro: 남사친 (namsachin) means a guy friend who is just a friend, not a boyfriend. Koreans use it in chats, dramas and dating talk to make that difference clear.
literal: It is short for 남자 사람 친구, "male person friend." The word 사람 (person) is added because 남자 친구 alone means "boyfriend."
usage: Use it when you want to say a man is a friend, not a romantic partner: 그냥 남사친이야 (He's just a guy friend).
Do not mix it up with 남친, which is short for 남자 친구 and means boyfriend.
It comes up a lot in dating talk, like whether a boyfriend minds his girlfriend's 남사친.
The female version is 여사친. It is casual, but not rude.

forms.note: Short for 남자 친구. Different meaning.

examples.context: Clearing up a misunderstanding
Telling a friend about your weekend
examples.en: I watched a movie with my guy friend.

examples.context: Asking for dating advice
examples.en: My boyfriend is jealous of my guy friend.

faq.q: What is the difference between 남사친 and 남친?
faq.a: 남친 means boyfriend. 남사친 means a male friend who is not your boyfriend.

faq.q: Why is 사람 in 남사친?
faq.a: Because 남자 친구 already means "boyfriend." Adding 사람 (person) makes it clear you just mean a friend who is a man.

intro: 여사친 (yeosachin) means a female friend who is just a friend, not a girlfriend. It is common in Korean chats, dramas and dating talk.
literal: It is short for 여자 사람 친구, "female person friend." The word 사람 (person) is added because 여자 친구 alone means "girlfriend."
usage: Use it to say a woman is a friend, not a partner: 그냥 여사친이야 (She's just a friend).
Do not confuse it with 여친, which is short for 여자 친구 and means girlfriend.
It often comes up when someone is jealous of their partner's female friends.
The male version is 남사친. It is casual, but not rude.

forms.note: Short for 여자 친구. Different meaning.

examples.context: Telling a friend what you did
examples.en: I ate with a female friend.

examples.context: A boyfriend explaining a photo
examples.en: She's just a friend, don't get the wrong idea.

examples.context: Complaining to a friend
examples.en: My boyfriend has too many female friends.

faq.q: What is the difference between 여사친 and 여친?
faq.a: 여친 means girlfriend. 여사친 means a female friend who is not your girlfriend.

faq.q: Can a woman call another woman her 여사친?
faq.a: It is mainly used across genders, like a man talking about a female friend. Between women, 친구 is the normal word.

intro: 엄친아 (eomchina) means a guy who seems perfect at everything: smart, good-looking and successful. Koreans use it in daily talk, variety shows and dramas, often for celebrities.
literal: It is short for 엄마 친구 아들, "mom's friend's son." The joke is that Korean moms often compare their kids to a friend's son who is always better at everything.
usage: It describes someone who has it all, like top grades, good looks and a great job.
It can be a compliment, but it often carries a little envy or a joke about being compared.
The female version is 엄친딸, short for 엄마 친구 딸 (mom's friend's daughter).
It is casual but friendly, and many people use it, including on TV.

forms.note: Another slang word with a similar idea.

examples.context: Describing a classmate who aces everything
A teen snapping at a nagging parent
examples.en: Don't compare me to some perfect kid!

examples.context: Reading about an actor's background
examples.en: Good at studying and sports too, he's a total golden boy.

faq.q: What does 엄친아 stand for?
faq.a: 엄마 친구 아들, meaning "mom's friend's son," the kid your mom always says is better than you.

faq.q: Is 엄친아 a compliment?
faq.a: Mostly, yes. It praises someone as good at everything, though it can come with a playful hint of envy.

meaning: Someone who falls in love fast
intro: 금사빠 (geumsappa) is slang for someone who falls in love very easily and very quickly. You hear it in variety shows, dating shows and chats when friends tease someone who has a new crush every week.
literal: It is short for 금방 사랑에 빠지는 사람, "a person who falls in love right away." 금방 means "right away," 사랑 is "love" and 빠지다 means "to fall into."
usage: People use it about friends, celebrities, or themselves: 나 금사빠야 means "I fall for people so easily."
It is light teasing, not a real insult. Said about yourself, it often sounds a little self-mocking.
It is casual slang, so keep it among friends and online. It would sound odd in a formal setting.
The opposite idea is someone slow to warm up, sometimes jokingly called 철벽 ("iron wall") when they block all romantic approaches.

forms.en: a person who falls in love right away
forms.note: The full phrase behind the abbreviation.
The ordinary verb for what a 금사빠 does often.

examples.context: Admitting your dating habits to a friend
examples.en: I fall for people way too easily.

examples.context: Teasing a friend with a new crush
examples.en: You fell for someone again? You really fall fast.

examples.context: Introducing yourself on a dating show
examples.en: I fall for people easily, so I often fall in love at first sight.

faq.q: What does geumsappa stand for?
faq.a: It stands for 금방 사랑에 빠지는 사람, which means "a person who falls in love right away."

faq.q: Is calling someone geumsappa rude?
faq.a: Not really. It is friendly teasing. Many people even use it to describe themselves.

intro: 모쏠 (mossol) is slang for someone who has never dated anyone in their life. You see it in dramas, dating shows and online posts, often in a joking, self-deprecating way.
literal: It is short for 모태솔로. 모태 means "mother's womb" and 솔로 is the English word "solo," meaning single. So the idea is "single since the womb," or single from birth.
usage: People mostly say it about themselves: 저 모쏠이에요 means "I've never dated anyone."
It is usually humorous, but calling someone else 모쏠 can sting if they are sensitive about it, so use it with friends who can take the joke.
You will also see it spelled 모솔. Both spellings are common online.
모쏠 탈출 ("escaping 모쏠") means finally getting your first boyfriend or girlfriend.

examples.context: Admitting it on a blind date
Making a New Year's resolution
examples.en: This year I'm definitely getting out of never-dated life.

examples.context: A friend reacting in disbelief
examples.en: You've really never dated? No way.

faq.q: What is the full form of mossol?
faq.a: It is 모태솔로, "single since the mother's womb," meaning someone who has never been in a relationship.

faq.q: Is it 모쏠 or 모솔?
faq.a: Both are used. 모솔 follows the spelling of 솔로 more closely, and 모쏠 matches how many people say it. Readers will understand either.

faq.q: Is mossol an insult?
faq.a: It is mostly used jokingly, especially about yourself. Pointing at someone else and calling them 모쏠 can come across as teasing or mean, depending on the person.

intro: 자만추 (jamanchu) is slang for wanting to meet a partner naturally, through everyday life, instead of blind dates or dating apps. You hear it on dating shows and in talk about love life.
literal: It is short for 자연스러운 만남 추구, "pursuing a natural meeting." 자연스러운 means "natural," 만남 means "meeting" and 추구 means "pursuit."
usage: People say 저는 자만추예요 or 자만추라서 to explain that they would rather meet someone at work, school or through hobbies than be set up.
The opposite is 인만추, short for 인위적인 만남 추구, "pursuing an arranged meeting," like 소개팅 blind dates or apps.
It is casual and a bit playful. It is common among people in their twenties and thirties.
People often joke that 자만추 is hard in adult life, since you rarely meet new people naturally.

forms.note: The opposite: blind dates and apps.
What a 자만추 person tends to avoid.

examples.context: Turning down a set-up from a friend
examples.en: I prefer to meet people naturally, so I don't do blind dates.

examples.context: Complaining about being single
examples.en: I want to meet someone naturally, but there's no one to meet.

examples.context: Talking about adult life
examples.en: These days meeting someone naturally is almost impossible.

faq.q: What does jamanchu stand for?
faq.a: 자연스러운 만남 추구, which means "pursuing a natural meeting." It describes people who want to meet a partner through daily life rather than set-ups.

faq.q: What is the opposite of jamanchu?
faq.a: 인만추, short for 인위적인 만남 추구. It means being open to arranged meetings such as blind dates and dating apps.

meaning: Someone who is all about looks
intro: 얼빠 (eolppa) is slang for someone who mainly cares about looks, especially a fan who likes a celebrity mostly for their face. You see it in K-pop fandom talk and casual chats.
literal: It combines 얼 from 얼굴 ("face") with 빠, a slang suffix for a devoted fan, taken from words like 빠순이 and 빠돌이. Together it means roughly "face fan."
usage: Fans say it about themselves: 나 얼빠야 means "I'm all about looks" or "I'm weak for a pretty face."
Said about others, it can sound like a mild dig, suggesting they are shallow. Among friends it is usually just teasing.
Do not mix it up with 얼빠지다 or 얼빠진, a standard expression meaning dazed or out of it. 얼빠진 사람 means "a dazed person," not a looks fan.
Related fandom slang includes 입덕 (becoming a fan) and 최애 (your favorite member).

forms.en: I admit I'm all about looks

forms.note: Different word. Standard Korean, not fandom slang.

examples.context: Explaining your taste in people
examples.en: I'm all about looks, so I'm weak for handsome people.

examples.context: Telling how you became a fan
examples.en: Honestly, at first I became a fan just for the face.

examples.context: Teasing a friend who only talks about looks
examples.en: Wow, you're totally all about looks.

faq.q: Is eolppa an insult?
faq.a: It is mild. Fans often call themselves 얼빠 with pride. Calling someone else 얼빠 can suggest they are shallow, so tone matters.

faq.q: Is eolppa the same as eolppajida?
faq.a: No. 얼빠지다 is a standard verb meaning dazed or absent-minded. 얼빠 is fandom slang for someone who likes people for their looks.

intro: 국룰 (gungnul, often typed gukrul) is slang for an unwritten rule that everyone follows, like "chicken goes with beer." You see it all over chats, comments and variety shows.
literal: It is short for 국민 룰, "the nation's rule." 국민 means "the people" or "the nation" and 룰 is the English word "rule." It is pronounced 궁눌, which is why the romanization is gungnul.
usage: People use it for habits that feel obvious or classic: 국룰이지 means "that's the rule, of course."
It is usually playful and about everyday things like food, school, games or how to celebrate.
It is casual slang. In polite speech you can still say 국룰이죠, but not in formal writing.
If you agree that something is a 국룰, you might reply ㅇㅈ ("I agree").

forms.note: The most common way to say it.

examples.context: Ordering fried chicken with friends
examples.en: Chicken with beer is the rule, obviously.

examples.context: Talking about birthday traditions
examples.en: Eating seaweed soup on your birthday is the rule.

examples.context: Explaining how to eat ramyeon
examples.en: With ramyeon, kimchi is the rule.

faq.q: What does gukrul stand for?
faq.a: 국민 룰, "the nation's rule." It means something everyone agrees is the standard way to do things.

faq.q: How do you pronounce 국룰?
faq.a: It sounds like gung-nul, because ㄱ followed by ㄹ changes in pronunciation. Many people still type it as gukrul in English.

intro: 소확행 (sohwakhaeng) means "small but certain happiness," the little everyday pleasures that make you happy. You see it in social media posts, ads and lifestyle articles.
literal: It is short for 소소하지만 확실한 행복, "small but certain happiness." The phrase comes from a Japanese expression used by the writer Haruki Murakami in an essay, and it became a popular trend word in Korea in the late 2010s.
usage: People use it for simple joys: a beer after work, sleeping in, a warm coffee. 이게 내 소확행이야 means "this is my little happiness."
Unlike most slang, it is fine in news articles and ads, so it is not limited to casual speech.
It carries a gentle, positive feel. It is about enjoying small things rather than chasing big goals.
A related trend word is 욜로 (YOLO), but 소확행 is calmer and about small moments.

forms.note: The last word in the phrase.

examples.context: Describing your routine
examples.en: A glass of beer after work is my little happiness.

examples.context: Enjoying a quiet moment
examples.en: This is what small happiness is.

examples.context: Talking about weekends
examples.en: Sleeping in on the weekend is my small happiness.

faq.q: What does sohwakhaeng stand for?
faq.a: 소소하지만 확실한 행복, "small but certain happiness."

faq.q: Is sohwakhaeng slang?
faq.a: It started as a trend word, but it is now common in articles, ads and everyday speech. You can use it with almost anyone.

intro: 내돈내산 (naedonnaesan) means "I bought it with my own money." Reviewers and influencers use it to say a review is honest and not sponsored.
literal: It is short for 내 돈 주고 내가 산, "bought by me with my own money." 내 돈 means "my money" and 내가 산 means "that I bought."
usage: It appears mostly in product reviews, blog titles, YouTube videos and social media captions, like 내돈내산 후기 ("self-paid review").
The point is trust: it tells readers no company paid for the post. It became popular because many reviews turned out to be hidden ads.
You can also say it in conversation when a friend asks if something was a gift: 아니, 내돈내산이야.
The opposite is a sponsored post, often called 협찬 (sponsorship) or 광고 (ad).

forms.en: bought by me with my own money

examples.context: Title of a blog review
examples.en: This is a review of something I bought with my own money.

examples.context: Answering a comment asking if it's an ad
examples.en: It's not an ad. I paid for it myself.

examples.context: Starting a video review
examples.en: I bought it myself, so I'll be honest.

faq.q: What does naedonnaesan stand for?
faq.a: 내 돈 주고 내가 산, "bought by me with my own money."

faq.q: Why do Korean reviewers write naedonnaesan?
faq.a: To show the review is not paid for. It tells readers the opinion is honest because no brand sponsored it.

intro: 꾸안꾸 (kkuankku) describes a look that is styled but seems effortless, like you did not try hard. You see it in fashion and makeup posts, shopping sites and celebrity airport-fashion articles.
literal: It is short for 꾸민 듯 안 꾸민 듯, "as if dressed up, as if not dressed up." 꾸미다 means "to dress up" or "to decorate," and 안 means "not."
usage: People use it for outfits, hair and makeup: 꾸안꾸 스타일, 꾸안꾸 메이크업.
It is a compliment. Saying someone's look is 꾸안꾸 means they look natural but put together.
People often joke that 꾸안꾸 takes more effort than it looks.
It is casual and very common in fashion content. It is used for both men and women.

forms.en: dressed up yet not dressed up

examples.context: Describing your outfit
examples.en: I dressed in an effortless style today.

examples.context: Getting ready in front of the mirror
examples.en: The effortless look is the hardest.

examples.context: Complimenting a friend's outfit
examples.en: Wow, it has a totally effortless vibe.

faq.q: What does kkuankku stand for?
faq.a: 꾸민 듯 안 꾸민 듯, which means "as if dressed up, as if not." It describes a natural but polished look.

faq.q: Is kkuankku a compliment?
faq.a: Yes. It means someone looks stylish without seeming to try too hard.

intro: 오운완 (ounwan, often typed owunwan) means "today's workout, done." It is a hugely popular hashtag on Korean Instagram, posted with gym selfies and workout photos.
literal: It is short for 오늘 운동 완료, "today exercise complete." 오늘 means "today," 운동 means "exercise" and 완료 means "completed."
usage: It is mostly written, as #오운완 on social media, often with a mirror selfie or a photo of a smartwatch.
You can also say it out loud to friends after the gym, like a small celebration: 오운완!
It is casual and upbeat. It is about showing consistency and motivating yourself and others.
People post an 인증샷 (proof photo) with it to show they actually worked out.

forms.note: A photo posted with the tag.

examples.context: Texting a friend after the gym
examples.en: Workout done! I did legs today.

examples.context: Telling a friend about your post
examples.en: I posted my workout-done proof photo.

examples.context: Caption on a gym selfie

faq.q: What does owunwan mean on Instagram?
faq.a: It is short for 오늘 운동 완료, "today's workout complete." People tag gym photos with #오운완.

faq.q: How is 오운완 romanized?
faq.a: The standard romanization is ounwan. Many people type owunwan because of how 운 is often spelled in English.

intro: 레전드 (rejeondeu) is the English word "legend" in Korean, used to call something legendary or epic. Fans use it for unforgettable stage performances, and people also use it for moments that were unbelievably bad.
literal: It is a loanword from English "legend." Korean adds a vowel after each final consonant, which turns legend into 레전드.
usage: Fans say 레전드 무대 ("legendary stage") or 레전드 짤 ("legendary meme image") for moments people will remember for years.
It can also be sarcastic. 오늘 레전드다 after a terrible day means "today was an epic disaster."
It is also used as a noun for a person who is a legend, like a famous athlete or a veteran singer.
Similar words are 대박 (awesome) and 역대급 (best or worst ever).

forms.note: Near-synonym for best or worst ever.

examples.context: Watching a live stage video
Talking about last night's match
After a day where everything went wrong
examples.en: Wow, today was an epic mess.

faq.q: Is rejeondeu always positive?
faq.a: No. It usually means amazing, but it can also mean an epic failure, depending on context and tone.

faq.q: Why is legend spelled 레전드?
faq.a: Korean has no consonant cluster like nd at the end of a word, so it adds a vowel, giving 레전드.

intro: 진심 (jinsim) means "sincerity" or "one's true heart," and in casual speech 진심? means "Seriously?" You hear it in drama confessions and constantly in chats, where people also say they are 진심 about a hobby.
literal: 진심 is a Sino-Korean word made of 진 (眞, "true") and 심 (心, "heart" or "mind"). So it literally means "true heart."
usage: As a normal word, it is serious: 진심으로 사과드립니다 means "I sincerely apologize." Confessions in dramas often include 진심이야 ("I mean it").
In casual talk, 진심? or 진심이야? means "Are you serious?" It works like 진짜? or 정말?
A newer slang use is ~에 진심이다, "to be really serious about something": 커피에 진심인 편 means "I'm kind of obsessed with coffee."
The basic word fits any register. The "seriously?" and "obsessed with" uses are casual.

examples.context: Hearing surprising news from a friend
A confession in a drama
Introducing your hobby

faq.q: What's the difference between jinsim and jinjja?
faq.a: Both can mean "seriously?" 진짜 means "real" or "really" and is more common. 진심 means "sincerity" and adds a feel of "do you truly mean it?"

faq.q: What does 'jinsim-in pyeon' mean?
faq.a: ~에 진심인 편 is a casual way to say you are really into something, like 운동에 진심인 편 ("I'm serious about working out").

intro: 어머나 (eomeona) means "Oh my!" and is a surprised exclamation. You hear it in K-dramas, often from mothers, aunts and older women, and it is also the title of a well-known trot song.
literal: It is a longer form of 어머, the classic Korean "oh!" of surprise. The extra 나 makes it sound a bit more drawn out and expressive.
usage: It is used for surprise, both good and bad: seeing a gift, hearing news, or noticing something shocking.
It is stereotypically said by women, especially middle-aged women. When men say it, it often sounds playful or comic.
It is an interjection, so politeness levels do not apply directly, but it sounds casual and is not used in formal speech.
Shorter 어머 is more common in everyday talk. 어머나 can sound a little old-fashioned or theatrical.

examples.context: Walking into a surprise party
examples.en: Oh my, what is all this?

examples.context: Someone sneaks up behind you
An aunt seeing her nephew after years
examples.en: Oh my, you've grown so much!

faq.q: What's the difference between eomeona and omo?
faq.a: 어머 (omo) is the short, everyday form. 어머나 is longer and more expressive, and can sound a bit dramatic or old-fashioned.

faq.q: Can men say eomeona?
faq.a: They can, but it is seen as a typically feminine exclamation, so from a man it often sounds playful or funny.

intro: 세상에 (sesange) is an exclamation like "Oh my god!" or "Good heavens!" used when something is shocking or amazing. You hear it a lot in K-dramas and from parents and grandparents.
literal: 세상 means "the world" and 에 means "in." So it literally means "in the world," a short way of saying something like "how could this happen in the world?"
usage: It is used for strong surprise, shock or amazement, both good and bad.
It suits almost anyone and any situation, since it contains no rude words. Older people use it a lot.
A stretched-out version is 세상에나, and a playful rhyming one is 세상에 마상에.
As normal grammar, 세상에 also just means "in the world," as in 세상에서 제일 ("the most in the world").

forms.note: Literal use of the same word.

examples.context: Seeing a messy, broken room
Checking the time late at night
examples.en: Oh my gosh, it's already ten?

examples.context: Opening a beautiful gift

faq.q: Is sesange religious like 'oh my god'?
faq.a: No. It does not mention God. It literally means "in the world," but it is used the way English speakers say "oh my god."

faq.q: Is sesange polite?
faq.a: It is safe to say around anyone. It is an exclamation, so it is not rude, though in very formal settings people usually keep reactions quiet.

intro: 아차 (acha) is what Koreans say when they suddenly realize a mistake, like "Oops!" or "Oh no, I forgot!" You hear it in dramas when a character remembers something too late.
literal: It is a native interjection with no deeper meaning in its parts. It simply expresses the moment you notice a slip.
usage: It is used for small mistakes and forgotten things: leaving your keys, saying the wrong thing, missing a stop.
아차 싶다 means "to have an oh-no moment," and 아차 하는 순간 means "in a moment of carelessness."
A repeated version, 아차차, sounds a bit lighter or more comic.
For a serious problem, people are more likely to say 큰일 났다 ("I'm in big trouble") or 어떡해 ("what do I do").

examples.context: Reaching the door and patting your pockets
examples.en: Oops, I left my wallet behind.

examples.context: Seeing rain outside the subway exit
examples.en: Oh no, I forgot my umbrella.

examples.context: Telling a friend about a mistake
examples.en: I had an oh-no moment, but it was already too late.

faq.q: What's the difference between acha and eotteokhae?
faq.a: 아차 is the instant "oops" when you notice a slip. 어떡해 means "what do I do?" and shows worry about what to do next.

faq.q: Is acha casual?
faq.a: It is an interjection, so it fits most situations. People say it to themselves more than to others.

intro: 에이 (ei) is a sound Koreans make to mean "aw, come on," "nah," or "oh, no way." You hear it in dramas and chats when someone doubts what they just heard or is mildly let down.
literal: 에이 is an interjection, a sound of reaction. It has no deeper parts or word origin to explain.
