usage: Use it when you do not believe something, as in 에이, 거짓말 (nah, you're lying), or when something small goes wrong, as in 에이, 아깝다 (aw, so close).
It is casual and friendly. Say it with friends, siblings or people your age. With elders or at work it can sound like you are brushing them off.
Do not mix it up with 에이씨, which adds a mild swear sound and shows real irritation. Plain 에이 is much softer.
Close reactions include 설마 (no way, surely not) and 아, 진짜 (oh, seriously).

forms.note: Rougher, shows annoyance. Avoid around elders.

examples.context: A friend says he just won the lottery
Missing the bus by a few seconds
A friend claims she is dating a celebrity

faq.q: Is 에이 rude?
faq.a: No. It is a light, casual sound. It can seem dismissive if you say it to an elder or your boss, so keep it for friends and family.

faq.q: What's the difference between 에이 and 에이씨?
faq.a: 에이 is mild doubt or disappointment. 에이씨 adds a sound like a soft swear word and shows real annoyance, so it is ruder.

faq.q: How do you use 에이 in a sentence?
faq.a: Put it at the start of your reaction: 에이, 설마 (no way), 에이, 아니야 (nah, it's not), 에이, 몰라 (ugh, whatever).

intro: 어휴 (eohyu) is a sigh in word form, like "ugh," "phew" or "geez." Koreans say it when they are tired, fed up or relieved, and drama parents say it a lot when their kids frustrate them.
literal: 어휴 copies the sound of a heavy breath out. It has no parts to break down. 휴 alone is a lighter "phew."
usage: It covers several feelings: tiredness (어휴, 힘들어), frustration (어휴, 답답해) and relief (어휴, 다행이다). Tone of voice tells you which.
It is casual. Sighing 어휴 straight at someone, especially an elder, shows you are fed up with them, so be careful.
아이고 is similar but wider, and older people use it more. 휴 is a lighter sigh of relief.

forms.note: Similar, used a lot by older people.

examples.context: After carrying heavy boxes up the stairs
A parent looking at a child's messy room
Hearing that a friend got home safely

faq.q: What's the difference between 어휴 and 아이고?
faq.a: Both can be sighs. 아이고 covers more situations, like pain, surprise and sympathy, and sounds a bit older. 어휴 is mostly tiredness, frustration or relief.

faq.q: Is it rude to say 어휴 to someone?
faq.a: It can be. Sighing 어휴 at a person shows you are annoyed with them. Saying it to yourself about a situation is fine.

intro: 우와 (uwa) means "wow!" It is the sound Koreans make when something amazes them, and you hear it all the time on variety shows, vlogs and in dramas.
literal: 우와 is an exclamation, a sound of amazement. It has no parts to break down. It is a longer, more drawn-out version of 와.
usage: Say it when you see something impressive, pretty, delicious or surprising.
It sounds a bit more excited and childlike than 와, so kids and excited adults use it a lot. You can stretch it out, like 우와아.
It is casual, but it is a reaction rather than speech to someone, so it is usually fine even around elders.
For stronger amazement people add 대박 (awesome) or 진짜 (really).

examples.context: Seeing a beautiful view from a mountain top
Opening a birthday present
A friend shows you a perfect test score

faq.q: What's the difference between 우와 and 와?
faq.a: They mean the same thing. 우와 is a little longer and more excited. 와 is quicker and used for everything from mild surprise to amazement.

faq.q: Do adults say 우와?
faq.a: Yes. It can sound a little cute or childlike, but adults say it all the time when they are genuinely impressed.

meaning: I know, right? / Tell me about it
intro: 그러게 (geureoge) means "I know, right?" or "tell me about it." Koreans say it to agree with something someone just said, and it is one of the most common replies in casual chats.
literal: 그러게 is built from 그렇다 (to be so, to be like that) with the ending -게. Taken together it is roughly "it is so."
usage: Use it to agree with a comment or complaint: if a friend says "it's so hot," you answer 그러게.
It can also mean "yeah, I wonder" when you share someone's puzzlement, as in 그러게, 왜 안 오지? (I know, why isn't he here?).
In 그러게 내가 뭐랬어 it means "see, what did I tell you," which can sound smug.
It is casual. Add 요 for 그러게요 with coworkers, strangers or elders.

forms.note: For people you speak politely to.

forms.en: see, what did I tell you

examples.context: A friend complains about the weather
examples.en: I know, it's way too hot.

examples.context: A coworker says the meeting went on forever
A friend is hungover after you told them to stop drinking
examples.en: See? What did I tell you?

faq.q: What's the difference between 그러게 and 맞아?
faq.a: 맞아 means "that's right" and confirms a fact. 그러게 shares a feeling, more like "I know, right?" It fits complaints and wondering better than facts.

faq.q: Is 그러게 polite?
faq.a: No, it is casual. Say 그러게요 to people you speak politely to, like coworkers or elders.

intro: 당연하지 (dangyeonhaji) means "of course!" Koreans say it to answer a question with a confident yes, and in dramas it is a classic reply to "do you love me?"
literal: 당연 comes from the Sino-Korean word 當然, meaning natural or obvious. 하다 makes it an adjective, and the ending -지 adds a sense of "of course, obviously."
usage: It answers yes questions with full confidence: "Are you coming?" "당연하지!"
It is casual, for friends, partners and family. With coworkers or elders say 당연하죠 or the softer 그럼요.
It can sound a little blunt if the question was a real request, because it hints the answer was obvious. 그럼 (sure) is a softer casual option.

forms.note: For people you speak politely to.
Adverb form, used inside a sentence.

examples.context: A friend asks if you will come to her wedding
A daughter asks her mom if she still loves her
A new employee asks a senior if she can ask questions later

faq.q: What's the difference between 당연하지 and 그럼?
faq.a: Both mean "of course." 당연하지 is stronger and stresses that the answer is obvious. 그럼 is softer, more like "sure."

faq.q: Can I say 당연하지 to my boss?
faq.a: Use 당연하죠 or 그럼요 instead. 당연하지 is casual speech and would sound too familiar.

faq.q: How do you write 당연하지 in English letters?
faq.a: The standard romanization is dangyeonhaji. The polite form 당연하죠 is dangyeonhajyo.

meaning: Oh well, it can't be helped
intro: 어쩔 수 없지 (eojjeol su eopji) means "oh well" or "it can't be helped." Koreans say it when they accept something they cannot change, and you hear it in dramas whenever plans fall through.
literal: 어쩌다 means to do something about a situation, -ㄹ 수 없다 means "cannot," and -지 adds a resigned "I guess." Put together: "there's nothing that can be done."
usage: Use it to shrug off a bad outcome: a sold-out show, a canceled trip, extra work you cannot refuse.
It sounds calm and accepting rather than upset. Adding 뭐 at the end, as in 어쩔 수 없지 뭐, makes it sound even more like a shrug.
It is casual. With coworkers or elders say 어쩔 수 없죠.
Do not confuse it with the slang 어쩔티비, which mocks someone. 어쩔 수 없지 is a normal, everyday phrase.

examples.context: The concert you wanted to see is sold out
examples.en: Oh well, let's go next time.

examples.context: Rain cancels a picnic
examples.en: It's raining, so it can't be helped.

examples.context: Coworkers told they must work on Saturday
examples.en: Nothing we can do, I guess.

faq.q: Is 어쩔 수 없지 the same as 어쩔티비?
faq.a: No. 어쩔 수 없지 is a normal phrase meaning "it can't be helped." 어쩔티비 is slang that mocks someone, like "so what?"

faq.q: Is 어쩔 수 없지 like "c'est la vie"?
faq.a: Close. Both accept something you cannot change. 어쩔 수 없지 is very everyday, used for small things like a closed restaurant as much as big ones.

intro: 잘했어 (jalhaesseo) means "good job" or "well done." Koreans say it to praise someone who did something well, and with the right tone it can also be a sarcastic "nice going."
literal: 잘 means "well" and 했어 is the casual past tense of 하다 (to do). Literally: "you did well."
usage: Parents say it to children, friends to friends, and teachers or seniors to juniors.
Praise in Korean usually goes from older to younger or senior to junior. Telling your boss 잘했어요 can sound like you are grading them, so people say 수고하셨습니다 (thank you for your hard work) instead.
Said flatly after a mistake, as in 아주 잘했네, it means "great job" in a sarcastic way.
잘한다 is used while someone is still doing something, like cheering them on.

forms.note: For people you speak politely to, but not to superiors.
Can be warm or sarcastic, depending on tone.

examples.context: A parent looking at a child's report card
A friend tells you she finally stood up to her rude boss
Your brother spills coffee on your laptop

faq.q: Can I say 잘했어요 to my teacher or boss?
faq.a: It is better not to. Praising a superior can sound like you are judging them. 수고하셨습니다 or 감사합니다 are safer.

faq.q: What's the difference between 잘했어 and 수고했어?
faq.a: 잘했어 praises the result: you did it well. 수고했어 thanks someone for their effort, whatever the result.

meaning: What's wrong with you? / Stop it
intro: 왜 이래 (wae irae) means "what's wrong with you?" or "why are you acting like this?" In dramas it is shouted in arguments, but it is also a playful "stop it!" between friends.
literal: 왜 means "why" and 이래 is a short form of 이러해, from 이러다 (to act like this). Literally: "why like this?"
usage: Use it when someone is acting strangely, teasing you, or doing something you do not like. Tone decides whether it is playful or angry.
It also works for things: 이거 왜 이래? means "what's wrong with this thing?" And 나 왜 이래 means "what's wrong with me?"
It is casual and can be confrontational. The polite 왜 이러세요? is what people say to a stranger who is bothering them, and it is still a sharp complaint.
왜 그래 is similar but asks about what someone is doing over there or what is bothering them, so it often sounds more concerned.

forms.note: Said to strangers, sounds like a protest.

examples.context: A friend teases you in front of your crush
Your laptop freezes again
A stranger grabs your arm on the street
examples.en: What do you think you're doing?

faq.q: Is 왜 이래 rude?
faq.a: It is casual and can sound angry. Between friends it is often playful. Never say it to an elder or your boss.

faq.q: What's the difference between 왜 이래 and 왜 그래?
faq.a: 왜 이래 reacts to what is happening right here, often with annoyance. 왜 그래 often asks what is wrong, and can sound more caring.

intro: 뭐라고 (mworago) means "what did you say?" or a shocked "what?!" Koreans use it when they did not hear something, and in dramas it is the classic reaction to shocking news.
literal: 뭐 means "what" and 라고 is a marker for quoting what someone said. Literally: "(you said) what?"
usage: Said with a rising, curious tone, it just means you did not catch what was said.
Said sharply, it means "excuse me?!" and shows shock or anger, like when someone says something outrageous.
It is casual. With elders or strangers say 네? or 뭐라고 하셨어요? (what did you say?). 뭐라고요? is polite in form but often sounds irritated.
뭐래 is a related slang reaction meaning "what is he even saying," used to dismiss nonsense.

forms.note: Can sound annoyed, so use carefully.

examples.context: Talking to a friend on a noisy street
Your sister admits she broke your new phone
You did not hear a shop clerk's question

faq.q: Is 뭐라고 rude?
faq.a: Not between friends. To elders or strangers it sounds too blunt. Say 네? or 뭐라고 하셨어요? instead.

faq.q: What's the difference between 뭐라고 and 뭐야?
faq.a: 뭐라고 is about something someone said. 뭐야 reacts to a thing or situation, like "what is this?" or "what the heck?"

intro: 아기 (agi) means "baby." It is the normal word for an infant, and Koreans also use it for baby animals, as a pet name for a partner, and for young idols fans want to protect.
literal: 아기 is a native Korean word for a baby. In speech it is very often pronounced 애기.
usage: The basic meaning is a real baby: 아기가 자요 (the baby is sleeping).
Put it before an animal to mean a young one: 아기 고양이 (kitten), 아기 강아지 (puppy).
Couples call each other 아기야 or, more often, 애기야 as a sweet nickname. This is cute between partners and odd with anyone else.
아가 is a related form used to call a baby. Some mothers-in-law also call their daughter-in-law 아가 as a term of affection.

forms.note: Spoken form, very common, also a pet name.
Calling a baby or a partner.
Used to call a baby; also by some in-laws.
아기 before an animal means its young.

examples.context: Visiting a friend's newborn
Whispering to someone who just walked in
Pointing at a pet shop window

faq.q: What's the difference between 아기 and 애기?
faq.a: They are the same word. 아기 is the standard spelling and 애기 is how most people say it. 애기 is also more common as a pet name.

faq.q: Can I call my girlfriend or boyfriend 아기?
faq.a: Yes, many couples use 아기야 or 애기야 as a sweet nickname. It is only for a partner, not for friends.

intro: 사모님 (samonim) means "madam" or "ma'am." It is a respectful title for the wife of a teacher, boss or other respected man, and in dramas it is what staff call the rich lady of the house.
literal: 사모 comes from the Sino-Korean 師母, "teacher's wife" (師 teacher, 母 mother). 님 is an honorific suffix.
usage: Originally it meant your teacher's wife. Today it is used for the wife of your boss, professor, pastor or other senior figure.
In dramas, housekeepers, drivers and employees call the wealthy wife of a chaebol family 사모님.
Shop staff and salespeople often call middle-aged women customers 사모님 as flattery. It sounds more respectful than 아줌마, which can be rude.
It is a title used to address or refer to someone. A woman would not call herself 사모님.

forms.note: The husband's title in many workplace uses.
Without 님, used when referring, less respectful.
Common in workplace and drama talk.

examples.context: An employee greeting the boss's wife
A housekeeper in a wealthy household
A clothing store clerk helping a customer
examples.en: Ma'am, this color looks great on you.

faq.q: Who do you call 사모님?
faq.a: The wife of your teacher, boss or another respected man. Salespeople also use it for middle-aged women customers to be polite.

faq.q: Is 사모님 better than 아줌마?
faq.a: Yes, when speaking to someone directly. 아줌마 can sound rude to a woman you do not know, while 사모님 sounds respectful, even flattering.

intro: 이모님 (imonim) is the honorific form of 이모, "aunt on your mother's side." Koreans use it to politely address women working in restaurants and women who work as nannies or housekeepers.
literal: 이모 means a maternal aunt, your mother's sister. 님 is an honorific suffix that adds respect.
usage: In casual restaurants, customers call the middle-aged woman serving them 이모 or 이모님. It feels warmer than 저기요 (excuse me).
Families call a nanny, housekeeper or caregiver 이모님. It is the normal respectful way to refer to her.
이모님 is more respectful than plain 이모. Regulars at a restaurant often drop the 님 once they feel close.
If you are unsure, 저기요 or 여기요 is always a safe way to get staff attention.

forms.note: Casual form, also a real maternal aunt.
The male counterpart, used for male staff.

examples.context: Ordering at a small Korean restaurant
examples.en: Ma'am, one bottle of soju here, please.

examples.context: A mother telling her husband about the nanny
Leaving a restaurant after a good meal

faq.q: Why do Koreans call restaurant staff 이모?
faq.a: It treats the server like a family member, which feels warm and friendly. It is especially common in casual, family-run places.

faq.q: What's the difference between 이모 and 이모님?
faq.a: 이모님 adds the honorific 님, so it is more polite. Use 이모님 with someone you do not know well.

faq.q: Is it okay for a foreigner to say 이모님?
faq.a: Yes. Staff usually find it friendly. If it feels unnatural, 저기요 works too.

intro: 막둥이 (makdungi) means the youngest child of a family, said with a lot of affection, like "the baby of the family." You hear parents and grandparents use it in dramas, often for a child born years after the others.
literal: 막 is the same part as in 막내 (the youngest), and -둥이 is a suffix for a person with some trait, as in 쌍둥이 (twins) or 귀염둥이 (cutie).
usage: Parents and grandparents call their youngest child 막둥이, even when that child is an adult.
It is warmer and more doting than 막내, which is a plain word for the youngest in any group, like a family, team or K-pop group.
People often add 우리, as in 우리 막둥이 (our little one).
It is also a popular name for a family's youngest pet.

forms.note: Neutral, used for families and groups.
A child born when the parents are older.

examples.context: A grandmother calling her youngest grandchild
A mother introducing her son to guests
examples.en: This is the baby of our family.

examples.context: A mother seeing her son off to military service
examples.en: My youngest is already off to the army.

faq.q: What's the difference between 막둥이 and 막내?
faq.a: Both mean the youngest. 막내 is neutral and works for any group, including K-pop groups and workplaces. 막둥이 is affectionate and used mostly by family.

faq.q: Can 막둥이 be used for pets?
faq.a: Yes. Many families call their youngest pet 막둥이, and it is also a common pet name.
